introduction-giving-ai-long-term-memory.core: LLMs know only their training data (frozen at a cutoff) and have limited context windows. Vector databases give them long-term, searchable memory of your documents, retrieved by meaning and fed into prompts (RAG).

first_principles.problem: An LLM can't answer questions about your company's internal docs, and it hallucinates instead.
truths: Training data is frozen and generic.
Context windows are finite and costly.
Relevant facts can be retrieved on demand.
derivation: Convert docs to **embeddings**.
Store them in a **vector database**.
**Retrieve** the most similar chunks per question.
**Augment** the prompt (RAG); search efficiently with **ANN indexes**.

analogy.title: A brilliant student without the textbook
analogy.story: Smart, but wrong on specific facts until allowed to look things up.
analogy.breaks: Retrieval quality limits answer quality: garbage in, garbage out.

example.title: An internal policy question
flow: Without: LLM invents a refund policy
With RAG: retrieves policy doc chunk

check.q: Why do LLMs need an external memory like a vector database?
check.a: Their knowledge is frozen at training time and their context is limited, so relevant private or current facts must be retrieved at query time.

the-core-idea-embeddings.core: An embedding model converts text (or images) into a dense vector of numbers where similar meanings sit close together in space. Similarity is measured with cosine similarity or dot product, so search becomes geometry.

first_principles.problem: Keyword search misses 'how do I get my money back?' when the doc says 'refund policy'.
truths: Meaning can be represented numerically.
Similar concepts cluster.
Distance metrics quantify similarity.
derivation: **Chunk** documents (e.g. 300–800 tokens, with overlap).
**Embed** each chunk with the same model.
**Store** vectors + metadata.
**Query**: embed the question, find the nearest vectors.

analogy.title: A map of meanings
analogy.story: Words are placed on a map so 'king' is near 'queen' and 'refund' is near 'money back'.
analogy.breaks: Embeddings carry their model's biases and blind spots, and changing models requires re-embedding.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Search by meaning, not exact words.

code.text:
q = embed("how do I get my money back?")
d = embed("Refund policy: customers may request a refund within 30 days")
cosine(q, d)  # ≈ 0.82 → highly related, despite no shared keywords

points: Same model for docs and queries.

check.q: Why must queries and documents be embedded with the same model?
check.a: Different models produce incompatible vector spaces, so distances between them would be meaningless.

rag-architecture-the-open-book-test.core: Retrieval-Augmented Generation: embed the user question, retrieve the top-k relevant chunks from the vector database, insert them into the prompt as context, and have the LLM answer from that context, ideally citing the sources. It's an open-book exam.

first_principles.problem: Fine-tuning an LLM on frequently changing documents is slow and expensive, and it still hallucinates.
truths: Context provided at query time grounds answers.
Documents change frequently.
Citations build trust.
derivation: **Ingest**: chunk → embed → store (with metadata).
**Retrieve**: query embedding → top-k (+ filters, hybrid search, reranking).
**Augment**: build the prompt with the chunks.
**Generate**: answer + cite, and refuse when the context is insufficient.

analogy.title: An open-book test
analogy.story: The student looks up the relevant pages, then writes an answer based on them.
analogy.breaks: Bad chunking or retrieval leads to confident wrong answers, so evaluate retrieval quality.

example.title: A minimal RAG loop

code.text:
chunks = vdb.search(embed(question), k=5, filter={"team": "hr"})
prompt = f"Answer using only this context. Cite sources.\n{format(chunks)}\nQ: {question}"
answer = llm.generate(prompt)

example.outcome: LLM apps grounded in your knowledge.

check.q: Why is RAG often preferred over fine-tuning for knowledge that changes frequently?
check.a: Updating the vector store is quick and cheap, while retraining models is slow and costly, and RAG supports citations.

the-challenge-of-search-indexing-algorit.core: Exact nearest-neighbour search compares the query with every vector, which is O(n) and too slow for millions or billions of vectors. Approximate Nearest Neighbour (ANN) indexes trade a little accuracy (recall) for orders-of-magnitude speed.

first_principles.problem: Brute-force search over 100 million 1,536-dimensional vectors takes seconds per query.
truths: Distance computations are expensive in high dimensions.
Near-perfect recall is usually enough.
Indexes structure space to skip most comparisons.
derivation: **Exact (flat)**: perfect recall, O(n).
**ANN**: partition or graph-structure the space.
Measure the **recall vs latency** trade-off.
Tune parameters (nprobe, ef_search).

analogy.title: Finding a book in a huge library
analogy.story: Checking every book is exact but slow; using sections and signposts is fast and almost always right.
analogy.breaks: ANN can miss the true nearest neighbour; for critical exact needs use flat search on small sets.

example.title: Brute force vs ANN
example.outcome: you understand why vector databases use ANN.

check.q: What trade-off do ANN indexes make?
check.a: They accept slightly lower recall (sometimes missing the true nearest neighbour) for dramatically faster search.

indexing-algorithm-1-ivf-inverted-file-i.core: IVF clusters the vectors (k-means) into partitions with centroids. At query time it compares the query only with the nearest few centroids (nprobe) and searches only those partitions. It's often combined with product quantization (IVF-PQ) for memory efficiency.

first_principles.problem: Comparing against every vector is too slow, but you need a structure that's simple and memory-efficient.
truths: Similar vectors cluster.
Searching nearby clusters finds most neighbours.
More probes means better recall but slower search.
derivation: **Train** k-means to get N centroids.
**Assign** each vector to its nearest centroid list.
**Query**: find the nprobe closest centroids, then search those lists.
Add **PQ** compression for large scale.

analogy.title: A librarian sorting books by subject
analogy.story: You go to the 'History' and 'Politics' sections only, not every shelf.
analogy.breaks: Vectors near cluster boundaries can be missed with low nprobe, and clusters need retraining if data shifts.

code.text:
quant = faiss.IndexFlatL2(d)
index = faiss.IndexIVFFlat(quant, d, 4096)   # 4096 clusters
index.train(xb); index.add(xb)
index.nprobe = 16                              # search 16 clusters
D, I = index.search(xq, 10)

check.q: What does the nprobe parameter control in IVF?
check.a: How many nearest clusters are searched per query, trading speed for recall.

indexing-algorithm-2-hnsw-hierarchical-n.core: HNSW builds a multi-layer graph: sparse upper layers act as highways for long jumps and dense lower layers handle local search. A query greedily navigates from the top layer down to its nearest neighbours, giving excellent recall and low latency.

first_principles.problem: Cluster-based indexes miss boundary neighbours, and you need very high recall at millisecond latency.
truths: Small-world graphs connect any two nodes in few hops.
Hierarchy speeds up long-distance navigation.
Graph search can be greedy and fast.
derivation: Insert each vector, connecting it to **M** neighbours.
Assign **random layers** (fewer nodes at higher levels).
**Search**: start at the top, descend greedily (ef_search candidates).
Tune **M, ef_construction and ef_search**.

analogy.title: Motorways, main roads and local streets
analogy.story: Take the motorway to the right region, then main roads, then local streets to the exact address.
analogy.breaks: HNSW uses lots of memory (graph links) and has costlier inserts and deletes.

check.a: It stores graph links (M neighbours per node, across layers) in addition to the vectors.

choosing-a-vector-database-the-landscape.core: Options range from vector extensions on existing databases (pgvector, OpenSearch, Elasticsearch) to purpose-built vector databases (Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, Milvus) and libraries (FAISS). Choose by scale, filtering needs, hybrid search, operations and existing stack.

first_principles.problem: Teams adopt a new specialised database when pgvector in their existing Postgres would have done the job.
truths: Scale requirements vary enormously.
Operational overhead matters.
Metadata filtering and hybrid search are often essential.
derivation: **< ~10M vectors + existing Postgres** → pgvector.
**Search + keyword needs** → OpenSearch/Elastic hybrid.
**Large scale or managed** → Pinecone, Qdrant, Milvus, Weaviate.
Evaluate **filtering, hybrid search, multi-tenancy, cost and ops**.

analogy.title: Choosing storage for your belongings
analogy.story: A cupboard at home (pgvector) is fine for most people; a dedicated warehouse (purpose-built DB) suits large collections.
analogy.breaks: Benchmarks vary with workload, so test with your own data and query patterns.

example.title: Two selection decisions
flow: Enterprise search, 500M vectors, multi-tenant → managed Milvus/Qdrant

check.q: When is pgvector often a good choice?
check.a: When you already run Postgres and have moderate vector volumes, which avoids running a new specialised system.
